public_rationale: The mechanism holds. Alethea's August 2025 investigation of a 400-account X network found that LLM-varied wording made detection more challenging than copypasta, which tools can easily match and flag. But 'no longer works' overstates the case. Alethea still detected that network through account attributes and posting behavior. Citizen Lab's October 2025 report on an AI-enabled network flagged its accounts partly because they shared the same content and identical hashtag strings. Copy-paste matching is weaker against swarms that truly vary their text, but it has not stopped working in practice.
limitations: The result depends on reading 'no longer works' as a strong claim. If it means 'no longer enough against AI swarms that vary every post', the claim would lean supported.
The evidence comes from two case studies, not a systematic measurement.

from_speaker: Because AI can now generate unique text for every single post
our_interpretation: Plain reading: detecting coordinated bot campaigns by matching identical or copy-pasted text is no longer an effective method, because AI-written posts vary their wording.
'No longer works' is read as a strong claim that the method has stopped being effective, not merely that it has become less effective.
The claim is present tense, so the period covers the months before the post.
criteria.support_condition: Credible investigations or studies show that AI-generated variation in wording defeats copy-paste or duplicate-text matching against recent bot networks, so detection has to rely on other signals.
criteria.contradiction_condition: Recent investigations show copy-paste or identical-content matching still identifying current, including AI-enabled, influence networks, or studies show that duplicate-text detection still catches AI-written campaigns.
